newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asia Grains - Buyers retreat to sidelines.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grains - Buyers retreat to sidelines.

text.p: East Asian grains buyers are seen being glued to the market sidelines this week, with Japanese corn buyers watching how export premiums will move in the near term, traders said on Monday.
"We'll be sidelined this week, although some will buy for July/September delivery," one Tokyo trader said. "We're watching how the volatile soybean market will affect the corn market."
Japanese corn buyers have covered up to 30 percent of their July/September shipments with U.S. corn. Premiums were quoted at about 94 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT May contract.

"We don't expect any inquiries for corn purchases from our clients this week as they will take a break after covering their needs for far forward shipments to August," a trader with Cheiljedang Corp in South Korea said.

The only business may be provided by South Korean flour makers Daehan Flour Mills Co Ltd and Korea Flour Milling Corp, who are expected to invite tenders this week to buy about 40,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for shipment in June, traders said.
Taiwanese buyers are also seen tendering in the next two weeks for two 34,000-tonne wheat shipments for late April to early June delivery.

Taiwanese feed producers are seen out of the market for the time being as they try to trim their corn inventories which have been badly affected by the sharp drop in demand caused by the hog epidemic which has hit the country's pork exports.
"Corn and soybean inventories are still too high," Taiwan Formosa Oilseed manager Steven Kuo told Reuters.

Taiwanese grain importers have said they expect corn imports to fall about 1.2 million tonnes, or equivalent to about 19 percent of the island's imports of 6.5 million tonnes a year, because of the epidemic.
Philippine grain importers are not likely to be in the market this week as they have ample supplies after a recent spate of orders, traders said.
The most recent purchase was for 60,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat and 15,000 tonnes of soybeans, traders said.

Freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest to Taiwan were pegged at about US$14.00 a tonne and from the U.S. Gulf at between $24.00 and $24.50 a tonne, both for Panamax-sized March shipments, Taiwanese dealers said.
In South Korea, a trader with the NLCF said the freight rate from the Pacific Northwest was steady at $15.50 a tonne. The rate from the U.S. Gulf was also unchanged at $25.50 a tonne.
